findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF pp.3–4, printed pp.2–3, Remark and continuation
findings.claim: The remark says f(x)=sin x, then takes G=∫cos t dt=sin x and F=sin x+21; the continuation displays ∫sin x dx=sin b−sin a.
findings.correction: Use f(x)=cos x and ∫cos x dx throughout this illustration. Alternatively an actual sine illustration needs G=1−cos x and a corresponding antiderivative.
findings.check: (sin x+21)′=cos x. With a=0,b=π, ∫sin x dx=2 but sin π−sin 0=0.

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF pp.4–5, printed pp.3–4, 200-digit-prime application
findings.claim: The interval [10^200,10^201] is described as counting 200-digit primes.
findings.correction: For 200-digit integers use [10^199,10^200); the shown interval concerns 201-digit integers, with power-of-ten endpoints composite.
findings.check: A positive integer n has 200 decimal digits exactly when 10^199≤n<10^200.

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF p.5, printed p.4, first line
findings.correction: The lower endpoint of the intended interval is 10^200 (or 10^199 if fixing the digit count).

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF p.5, printed p.4, last approximation of prime count
findings.claim: After claiming one significant figure, 9·10^200/500≈10^198 is displayed.
findings.correction: That expression is exactly 1.8·10^198, hence 2·10^198 to one significant figure. 10^198 is acceptable only as an order-of-magnitude label. Corrected 200-digit interval gives about 2·10^197 by the same rough method.

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF p.5, printed p.4, Bessel definition
findings.correction: Coefficient must be 1/π for these limits (or retain 1/(2π) and integrate over a full 2π interval).
findings.check: At x=0 the printed expression equals 1/2, whereas standard J0(0)=1. NIST DLMF 10.9.1 confirms the 1/π formula.

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF pp.4–5, printed pp.3–4, encryption prose
findings.claim: A secret prime is presented as what decodes messages and abundance of primes is used to infer bank-account security.
findings.correction: Treat this as a rough motivation, not a cryptographic security argument. RSA uses a public modulus/exponent and private exponent or factor-based CRT key representation; sheer prime count does not establish security.
findings.check: RFC 8017 §3.2 describes (n,d) or a factor/CRT representation. The calculus estimate alone contains no algorithmic attack-cost model.

findings.locator: lec20.pdf PDF pp.2–3 and p.5, printed pp.1–2 and p.4
findings.claim: Geometric proof uses ordinary positive area and positive Δx; Fresnel functions use cos(t²), sin(t²).
findings.correction: Extend FTC2 via signed integrals and both signs of the increment. Fresnel normalization is a valid unscaled convention; do not label it a mathematical error merely because standard DLMF C,S use πt²/2.
findings.check: Average difference quotient tends to f(x) by continuity on either oriented interval. Scaling u=sqrt(2/π)t relates the Fresnel conventions.

checked_deductions: FTC2: |(1/h)∫_x^(x+h)f(t)dt−f(x)|≤sup_{t between x and x+h}|f(t)−f(x)|→0 for either sign h.
FTC1: G′=f=F′ gives F−G constant on the interval, and G(a)=0.
C′(x)=cos(x²); S′(x)=sin(x²). The logarithmic-integral definition from 2 is ordinary only for x>1; the singularity at t=1 must not be crossed without a separate convention.
